## Overview

The Tsez, also known as the Dido or Didoi, are a North Caucasian ethnic group centered in the Tsunta district of the Republic of Dagestan, Russia. They inhabit the upper basin of the Andi Koysu in southwestern Dagestan, while smaller communities live elsewhere in Dagestan and in eastern Georgia. According to the 2002 Russian census, 15,256 people in Russia identified themselves as Tsez, including 15,176 in their homeland. Their unwritten language, Tsez or Dido, belongs to the Northeast Caucasian group and had 15,354 speakers in the cited demographic information. Tsez culture developed in a mountainous environment where seasonal livestock rearing, terraced cultivation, village institutions, multilingualism, and Sunni Islam shaped everyday life.

## Festivals & rituals

 They state that Islam gradually became established among the Tsez, with Islamization intensifying from the 15th century and Islam becoming dominant by the 17th–18th centuries. Elements of earlier religious practices survived alongside Islamic beliefs, and the Tsez adhere to Sunni Islam.

## Foodways

The Tsez traditional economy was adapted to a mountainous environment. Abundant pastureland and limited arable land supported seasonal livestock rearing, particularly sheep raising, while cattle and horses were also kept. Agriculture was practiced on terraced fields, but local grain production was insufficient to meet requirements, so agricultural products were exchanged with communities in the lowlands.

## Oral tradition & literature

Tsez lacks a literary tradition and is poorly represented in written form. Attempts have nevertheless been made to develop a stable orthography, mainly for recording traditional folklore. A collection of Tsez folklore texts written in the Mokok dialect was in production in the source material.

## Language & religion

Tsez, also called Dido, is an unwritten Northeast Caucasian language spoken by the Tsez in the mountainous Tsunta District of southwestern Dagestan. The language is also referred to in Tsez as *цезйас мец* (*cezyas mec*) or *цез мец* (*cez mec*). Its dialects include Asakh (*Asaq*), Tsebari (*Ceboru*), Mokok (*Newo*), Kidero (*Kidiro*), Shaytl (*Ešiƛʼ*), Shapikh (*Šopix*), and Sagada (*Soƛʼo*). Hinukh and Khwarshi were once regarded as dialects but are now commonly viewed as distinct languages of the same family. Avar and Russian serve as literary languages locally; Tsez is not taught in school, where Avar is taught for the first five years and Russian afterwards. In 1993, Mikhail Alekseev devised an orthography for Tsez, and in 2023 the letter ГӀ гӀ was added. Tsez grammar was first analyzed by the Georgian linguist Davit Imnaishvili in 1963. The language has four noun classes in the singular and two in the plural, an ergative–absolutive structure, eight syntactical cases, and a much larger number of locative cases. The Tsez adhere to Sunni Islam, while elements of pre-Islamic religious practice remain present.
